# Matthew 8 (BSB): research notes for a verse-by-verse commentary

**How to use these notes.** Every point below comes from a page I read, with its URL. Some verses have little or no coverage because of limits on my searches and page reads:

- The Spurgeon commentary page cut off at v. 26.
- The Utley commentary on bible.org cut off at v. 19.
- For the Guzik commentary (enduringword.com), I only read vv. 1–10 in full. A few later points come from its search summary.

Gaps worth filling before you publish:
- **No sources found:** vv. 27, 29, 33, 34. Verse 32 has only one line, from Wesley.
- **No Lutheran or Orthodox sources** found.
- **Nothing from netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org.** I couldn't check the NET notes on the Gadarenes/Gerasenes name.

---

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**Overview of chs. 8–9**
- Utley: chapters 8 and 9 form a unit of ten miracles showing Jesus' authority over people, disease and nature. They are placed right after the Sermon on the Mount on purpose. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21274
- Guzik, quoting Carson: Matthew arranges this material by topic, not in time order. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-8/

**v. 1** (crowds follow him down the mountain)
- Utley: this verse and 5:1 frame the Sermon. Some see Jesus as a second lawgiver like Moses, except that he *gives* the new law rather than receiving it. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21274
- Spurgeon: curiosity drew the crowd, and Jesus never valued popularity for its own sake. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-8-commentary-spurgeon

**v. 2** (the leper kneels: "if You are willing")
- Guzik: the Greek verb for kneeling/worship is used of homage to the divine. Guzik notes this is the first time anyone in Matthew calls Jesus "Lord." The leper doubts Jesus' willingness, not his power. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-8/
- Spurgeon: Jesus accepted worship he would have refused if he were merely a good man. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-8-commentary-spurgeon
- Utley takes a more cautious view: "Lord" (*kurios*) can mean just "Sir," and here the meaning is unclear. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21274
- Matthew Henry: Jesus begins with a leper because leprosy was seen as a particular mark of God's displeasure, showing he came to turn away God's wrath by taking away sin. https://studylight.org/commentaries/mhm/matthew-8.html

**v. 3** ("I am willing… Be clean!")
- Calvin: under the Law, touching a leper made a person unclean. But Christ's purity repel[s] all filth and defilement. He could have healed by word alone; the touch expressed compassion. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/matthew-8.html
- Utley: the touch went against Lev. 13:45–46 and showed Jesus' compassion and lack of fear. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21274
- Guzik: Jesus usually chose the way of healing that would mean most to the person. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-8/

**v. 4** ("tell no one… show yourself to the priest")
- Clarke: if Jesus had been openly proclaimed Messiah this early, the crowds would likely have tried to make him king, which would have stirred up both the Jewish rulers and Rome. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/matthew-8.html
- Utley calls this the "Messianic secret": Jesus did not want to be known simply as a healer. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21274
- Calvin: the priest would officially confirm the healing, and the offering was the man's thanksgiving. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/matthew-8.html
- Spurgeon: Jesus honoured the old law while it still stood. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-8-commentary-spurgeon

**vv. 5–6** (the centurion's request)
- Utley: no one in Jewish society was more shunned than lepers and Roman officers. Luke 7:1–10 tells the same story in a different setting. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21274
- Calvin: Luke says the centurion sent Jewish elders, but there is no contradiction. Matthew simply credits the centurion with what was done in his name. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/matthew-8.html
- Clarke: from Luke 7:5, the centurion was probably a devout Gentile who believed in Israel's God without being circumcised. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/matthew-8.html
- Spurgeon: the centurion lays out the case without telling Jesus what to do. "Not merit, but misery" is the plea. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-8-commentary-spurgeon

**v. 7** ("I will go")
- Utley: the "I" is emphatic. Entering a Gentile's home was a serious cultural and religious taboo. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21274
- Guzik: this was against Jewish custom but not against God's law. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-8/

**vv. 8–9** ("I am not worthy… just say the word")
- Ellicott: the centurion's sense of unworthiness involved the consciousness of his own sins, and the recognition of the surpassing holiness and majesty of Jesus. https://biblehub.com/matthew/8-8.htm
- Calvin: it is unlikely the centurion fully understood Christ's divinity. But he credited the power to God's word, and believed Christ was God's minister. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/matthew-8.html
- Utley: other healers used chants and rituals, while Jesus healed by his spoken word. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21274
- Matthew Henry contrasts this with the friends who carried the paralytic: Christ praised theirs as a *working* faith and the centurion's as a *trusting* faith. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_008.cfm

**v. 10** (Jesus marvels)
- Spurgeon: Jesus praised the centurion to the crowd, not to his face. Great faith can grow where there is little soil. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-8-commentary-spurgeon

**vv. 11–12** (east and west; outer darkness)
- Utley: Gentiles are being brought into God's family, pictured as the Messianic banquet (Isa. 25:6–9). "Outer darkness" and "weeping and gnashing of teeth" describe separation from God in hell. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21274
- Wesley: "outer darkness" alludes to the ancient custom of making their feast in the night time (so those shut out stand in the dark). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/matthew-8.html
- Spurgeon: those nearest are cast out and those furthest brought near. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-8-commentary-spurgeon

**v. 13** ("As you have believed")
- Spurgeon: the Lord often gives in proportion to faith. Going home is itself taking Jesus at his word. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-8-commentary-spurgeon

**vv. 14–15** (Peter's mother-in-law)
- Utley: Peter was married (1 Cor. 9:5). https://bible.org/book/export/html/21274
- Spurgeon: the cure was immediate and complete; serving is the proof of healing. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-8-commentary-spurgeon

**v. 16** (evening; many healed)
- Utley: evening marked the end of the Sabbath (Mark 1:32). The NT always distinguishes demon possession from disease. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21274

**v. 17** (Isaiah 53:4)
- Utley: the quote matches neither the Hebrew nor the Greek Old Testament, and this is the only NT citation of the verse. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21274
- Vincent's Word Studies: the verb means "he bore," as a burden laid upon him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/8-17.htm
- Ellicott: Jesus suffered with those he saw suffer, and healing left him physically exhausted. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/8-17.htm
- Spurgeon makes a similar point: healing drained his strength. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-8-commentary-spurgeon
- Gill raises the difficulty: Isaiah speaks of Christ's sufferings, and of the diseases of the mind, of sins, as the Apostle Peter interprets it. https://www.studylight.org/bible/lat/cvl/matthew/8-17.html

**v. 18** (crossing to the other side)
- Spurgeon: Jesus was moving away from popularity. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-8-commentary-spurgeon

**vv. 19–20** (the scribe; "no place to lay His head")
- Utley: scribes were experts in the oral and written law; most were Pharisees. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21274
- Spurgeon: the scribe's offer was an impulse Jesus had not asked for. Jesus tests it by pointing to his own poverty. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-8-commentary-spurgeon

**vv. 21–22** ("let the dead bury their own dead")
- Most commentators read the first "dead" as the spiritually dead:
  - Ellicott: the contrast between the two meanings of the word "dead." https://biblehub.com/matthew/8-22.htm
  - Gill: Jesus is not speaking against burying the dead; this disciple simply had a higher calling. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/hnv/matthew/8-22.html
  - Clarke: Jews spoke of a lawbreaker as a "dead man," so the saying was familiar. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/lsb/matthew/8-22.html
  - Barnes: the sternness may have been a test of the man's commitment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/8-22.htm
- Was the father already dead?
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB): probably an aged father the son wanted to see buried before leaving. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/8-22.htm
  - Wesley: It is not certain that his father was already dead. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/matthew-8.html
- Spurgeon: "The first man was too fast, the second was too slow." https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-8-commentary-spurgeon

**vv. 23–26** (the storm)
- Spurgeon:
  - Being in the boat with Jesus does not exempt anyone from storms.
  - Jesus slept because he trusted his Father.
  - Jesus rebuked the disciples first and the wind second.
  - "Little faith" is precious because it is faith, but blameworthy because it is little.
  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-8-commentary-spurgeon

**v. 28** (Gadarenes; two demon-possessed men)
- The place name varies by manuscript:
  - A Bible Hub dictionary entry says "Gadarenes" is the best-attested reading in Matthew. https://biblehub.com/dictionary/g/gadarenes.htm
  - The ESV footnote lists the other readings: Some manuscripts Gergesenes; some Gerasenes. https://www.blueletterbible.org/verse/esv/mat/8/28/
- Two men or one? Wesley: Mark and Luke mention only one, who was probably the fiercer of the two; this does not contradict Matthew. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/8.htm

**vv. 30–32** (the pigs)
- Wesley:
  - Jews were not allowed to keep pigs, so Jesus both justly and mercifully permitted them to be destroyed.
  - "Go" was a word of permission only, not command.
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/8.htm

---

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

**v. 17: Is physical healing "in the atonement"?** This is the clearest disagreement in the chapter.
- **Charismatic Reformed (Sam Storms):**
  - Every healing is the fruit of Christ's death, But it does not necessarily follow that where there is atonement there is *always* an immediate healing. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/is-there-healing-in-atonement
  - He suggests saying healing comes *through* the atonement rather than *in* it, to avoid implying healing is guaranteed in this life. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/physical-healing-atonement/
- **Pentecostal (Assemblies of God):** the AG publishes a paper by Anthony Palma, "Healing and the Atonement," which studies the Greek words in v. 17. I only saw an excerpt, so I can't report its conclusion. https://ag.org/-/media/AGORG/Beliefs/DivineHealing/HealingandAtonement.pdf?la=en
- **Baptist (John MacArthur):** the atonement includes not only salvation of souls but the healing of our bodies ultimately. https://www.gty.org/sermons/42-66/only-god-forgives-sin-part-2
- **Evangelical (GotQuestions):** in Matthew 8 Jesus bore the *consequences* of sin, not sin itself. "Healed" in Isa. 53:5 and 1 Pet. 2:24 means forgiven. https://www.gotquestions.org/by-His-stripes-healed.html
- **Utley:** this verse is not enough to say all disease is outside God's will and will be cured with enough faith (2 Cor. 12:8–10; 2 Tim. 4:20). https://bible.org/book/export/html/21274

**vv. 2–3: May we assume Jesus is willing to heal?**
- **Guzik (enduringword):** assume Jesus is willing unless he shows otherwise, as with Paul's thorn in the flesh. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-8/
- **Older view (Sermon Bible Commentary):** the leper's faith in Christ's power was stronger than his faith in Christ's goodness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/sbc/matthew-8.html

---

## 3. Other views

**v. 8 (Catholic):** the centurion's words are echoed at Mass before Communion.
- A post on the Catholic Answers *forum* (user-written, not an official catholic.com article) explains the "roof" as the body, a temple of the Holy Spirit, and the believer as unworthy to receive Christ in the Sacrament. https://forums.catholic.com/t/i-am-not-worthy-to-receive-you/193256
- Augustine: by calling himself unworthy, the centurion showed himself worthy for Christ to come not into his house, but into his heart. https://biblehub.com/study/matthew/8-8.htm

**v. 14 (Protestant–Catholic point):** Spurgeon uses Peter's marriage as a jab at "the so-called successors of Peter," meaning the popes. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-8-commentary-spurgeon

**v. 17 (faith-healing / word of faith):**
- Storms sums up the view he rejects: if you are not healed, it's not because God doesn't will it, but because you don't believe it. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/physical-healing-atonement/
- Vincent calls v. 17 the corner-stone of the faith-cure theory. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/8-17.htm
- Utley notes that many modern groups use this verse to claim physical healing is part of the atonement. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21274
